Every SDET I know has a private ritual for the morning after a red nightly, and every one of them is embarrassed by it.

Mine went like this. Open the report. Count the failures. Scan the test names. Then, without opening a single stack trace, decide which ones were "probably real" based on nothing more defensible than a feeling about which parts of the app had been touched that week.

I called it triage. It was pattern matching on vibes, and I did it every working day for years.

The morning that made me stop

Nine failures. Here's what they turned out to be, after I'd spent most of a day finding out.

Four were a locator change. Someone had shipped a component refactor and a data-testid had moved. Test bug. Not a product bug. Twenty minutes to fix once I knew.

Two were the product. A genuine regression in address validation, shipped the previous afternoon, which would have blocked real customers from checking out in three countries.

Two were infrastructure. The grid had dropped sessions partway through. Nothing was wrong with anything.

One was test data. A fixture account had been consumed by an earlier run and never reset, so the test was operating on a user that no longer had the state it expected.

Four completely different categories of problem. Four completely different owners. Four completely different urgencies. One of them was worth waking someone up for and three of them were worth nothing at all.

In the report, all nine looked exactly the same. Nine rows. Same red. Same font.

I found the address validation bug seventh. I got to it around 3pm, because I'd worked down the list in the order the report happened to print them, which is to say alphabetically, which is to say randomly. It had been in production for twenty-two hours by the time anybody knew what it was.

Nothing about that was my failure of judgment. There was no judgment available to make. The information required to rank those nine failures did not exist anywhere in my toolchain.

Red is not a category

This is the thing I've come to believe and it took me an embarrassingly long time to phrase it properly.

A test failure is a claim that expected and actual diverged. That is all it is. But there are at least four fundamentally different explanations for that divergence:

The product is broken. The thing you're testing does the wrong thing. This is the only one anybody actually wants to hear about, and it's the one your report is worst at identifying.

The test is broken. The product is fine. Your locator is stale, your wait is too short, your assertion encoded an assumption that stopped being true. The product team owes you nothing here. This is your bug.

The environment is broken. The grid dropped a session, a container failed to pull, DNS hiccuped, the deploy hadn't finished when the suite started. Nobody's bug. Nothing to fix. Pure noise.

The dependency is unavailable. The Stripe sandbox was unreachable. The auth provider was rate limiting. Your test could not run, which is genuinely different from your test having run and failed. You have learned nothing about the product, but your report says you have, and what it says is "broken."

That fourth one is the most expensive category I know of. Blocked is not failed. A blocked test carries zero information about the product, but it renders identically to a failure that carries a lot. I have personally watched two engineers lose an afternoon to a P0 on a payments bug that did not exist, because CI could not reach a sandbox and the report had no vocabulary for saying so. The report only knew one word, and the word was red.

Why we all triage by vibes

I want to defend the ritual for a second, because it isn't laziness.

Given nine identical red rows and no distinguishing information, guessing based on recent commits is genuinely the highest expected value strategy available. If the checkout team shipped yesterday and a checkout test is red, that's a real Bayesian update. I wasn't being sloppy. I was doing inference with the only prior I had, because the evidence I actually needed had never been captured.

And the alternative was worse. The alternative was opening nine sets of artifacts and finding, in each one, a stack trace pointing at a line in a page object, a screenshot taken at teardown (which is to say after the failure, after the page had already moved on), and a video I'd have to scrub through. Fifteen minutes per failure to determine a category that the machine already knew at the moment of failure and simply threw away.

That's the part that still gets me. The runner knew. At the instant the test failed, the process had the DOM, the console, the network activity, the response codes, the session state. All of it existed in memory. Then it wrote a stack trace and a screenshot to disk, discarded the rest, and left me to reconstruct by hand what it had been holding a second earlier.

What actually helped

I never fully solved this, and I'd distrust anyone who claims they have. But four things moved the number, roughly in order of effort to payoff.

Fail fast on preconditions, and fail with a different word. Before the suite runs, check that every external dependency answers. If the payment sandbox is unreachable, the affected tests report BLOCKED, not FAILED, and the pipeline says so in the summary. This is a couple of hours of work and it removed an entire category of false alarm permanently. Most runners support a custom status or a skip-with-reason. Use it.

Capture the DOM at the moment of failure, not at teardown. A teardown screenshot shows you the aftermath. You want the state at the assertion. Most modern runners can hook this. It's the single highest value artifact for separating "the button wasn't there" from "the button was there and did the wrong thing."

Tag failures by exception type automatically. A stale element reference and a NoSuchElement are almost always test bugs. An assertion error on a value is much more likely to be a product bug. A timeout waiting for the app is ambiguous, but a connection refused to your own grid is not. You can classify a decent proportion of failures with a lookup table and no cleverness at all. It won't be perfect. It doesn't need to be perfect. It needs to be better than alphabetical.

Sort the report by blast radius, not by name. If a failure sits on a revenue path, it goes at the top. This requires you to have decided, in advance and in writing, which tests those are. That conversation is uncomfortable and worth having, because right now that ranking exists only in the head of whoever is on triage that morning.

The question I'd ask your team

Not "what's our pass rate." Everybody has that number and it means less than people think.

Ask this instead: when a test goes red, how long does it take us to know which of the four it is?

If the honest answer is measured in fifteen-minute increments per failure, multiply that by your average red run, and by the number of red runs per month. That's a real number, it's probably larger than you expect, and none of it appears on any report anybody shows leadership.

I was a competent engineer doing archaeology every morning because the tooling recorded the conclusion and threw away the evidence. I don't think that's a personal failing. I think it's the default, and I think we're all quietly agreeing not to mention how much of the week it eats.

articles.title: The Astro Image Gotcha That Broke Our Production Build and How We Fixed It
articles.description: We ship a bilingual (French/Arabic) marketplace site built on Astro — static output, hundreds of...
articles.body_html:
We ship a bilingual (French/Arabic) marketplace site built on Astro — static output, hundreds of location plus service pages, and a few thousand professional profile pages, each with a photo pulled from Firebase Storage. Nothing exotic. Then one day the production build just... died. No warning during local dev, no failing test, no lint error. npm run build exited non-zero, and the stack trace pointed at astro:assets.

The cause, once I dug in: one profile's photo URL had gone stale. A Firebase Storage download token had rotated, so a request that used to return a JPEG now returned a 403. That's it. One dead URL, out of a few thousand, took the entire build down with it.

That surprised me, because I assumed Astro's image pipeline would fail soft on a bad remote image — log a warning, skip it, move on. It doesn't. Here's why, and what we did about it.

Why can't catch this

Astro's component and the underlying getImage() function both hand off to an Image Service, whose job is to transform() the image — resize it, convert format, whatever your config says. That's the part you can hook into and customize.

The problem is that transform() only ever receives an image that's already been fetched, as a raw buffer. The actual network request for a remote src happens earlier inside Astro's own internal loadRemoteImage step — whixh isn't part of the public, pluggable Image Service API. There's no supported hook that sits between "here's a remote URL" and "here's the fetched buffer" where you can intercept a failed request and decide what to do about it.

So from the framework's point of view, a 403 or a timeout on a remote image isn't a "handle this gracefully" situation — it's a fatal error during static generation. If even one image URL in your dataset is dead, the whole build stops.

The two-minute fix (and why it's not enough)

The fastest way out is obvious: swap for a plain tag. That sidesteps Astro's build-time fetch-and-transform step entirely, because a plain just emits the URL as-is and lets the browser deal with it at runtime.

That got our deploys unblocked immediately, but it's a real trade-off, not a fix — you lose automatic resizing, format conversion (WebP/AVIF), and the responsive srcset handling that's the entire reason to use in the first place. Fine as a stopgap. Not something to leave in place.

The actual fix: check before you build, not during

The real problem wasn't that Astro handles failures badly — it's that we were handing Astro URLs we hadn't verified. So we moved the verification earlier, into a prebuild step that runs before Astro ever touches an image.

The script is small: collect every unique remote image URL your pages will reference, HEAD-check each one with a timeout, and write the ones that fail to a JSON manifest.

js
// scripts/validate-image-urls.mjs
import fs from "node:fs";

const TIMEOUT_MS = 8000;
const CONCURRENCY = 10;

async function checkUrl(url) {
const controller = new AbortController();
const timer = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), TIMEOUT_MS);
try {
const res = await fetch(url, { method: "HEAD", signal: controller.signal });
return res.ok;
} catch {
return false; // timeout, DNS failure, connection reset — all treated as "bad"
} finally {
clearTimeout(timer);
}
}

Two design decisions mattered more than the code itself:

Fail closed per URL, fail open in aggregate. If a single URL times out or errors, treat it as bad — that's the safe default for one image. But if, say, 70% of all URLs fail in the same run, that's not "most of our images died overnight," that's almost certainly the checker itself being broken — offline CI runner, DNS hiccup, rate limiting. In that case the script leaves the existing manifest untouched rather than blanking every photo on the site. A partial network failure in your validation step shouldn't be able to nuke your production content.

Hook it in with prebuild, not an Astro integration. We wired this through npm's own lifecycle ("prebuild": "node scripts/validate-image-urls.mjs" in package.json), which runs automatically before build. We deliberately skipped writing it as an Astro integration hook — it's simpler, it's fully decoupled from Astro's internal build order, and it'd survive a framework migration untouched.

On the component side, it's a one-line check:

astro

import { isBadImageUrl } from "../utils/badImageUrls";

const showFallback = isBadImageUrl(profile.thumbnail);

{showFallback
? /* render an initials avatar instead / null
: / render the optimized Image component with profile.thumbnail as the source */ null}

Known-bad URLs get a graceful fallback (initials avatar) instead of ever reaching . Everything else gets the full optimization pipeline as normal.

Does it actually work at scale?

The first real production run checked several thousand unique image URLs against the live network in a few seconds thanks to the concurrency limit, and it did exactly what it was supposed to: flagged a handful of genuinely dead URLs, left everything else alone, and the build stopped depending on the uptime of every single image host on the internet.

One small habit that paid off while shipping this: when I reverted the emergency fallback back to once the validator was in place, I diffed against git history (git show HEAD:path/to/file) instead of trusting my memory of what the original props looked like. Cheap insurance — worth doing any time you're undoing an emergency fix under time pressure.

The takeaway

If you're using Astro's or getImage() with remote sources you don't fully control — user uploads, a CMS, cloud storage — don't assume a bad URL fails gracefully. It doesn't, by design, because the fetch happens in a part of the pipeline you can't hook into. Validate before the build starts, not during it.

We run this on bricoleapp.com, a bilingual home-services marketplace for Morocco and Egypt — happy to go deeper on any part of this if it's useful.

articles.title: Everyone's Adding AI to Everything. I Spent a Year Removing the Server Instead
articles.description: Open DEV's front page on basically any day right now and you'll find an AI-generated component tool,...
articles.body_html:
Open DEV's front page on basically any day right now and you'll find an AI-generated component tool, an AI prompt that "generates production-ready code," or a chatbot bolted onto something that didn't have one last month. I'm not writing this to dunk on any of that — some of it is genuinely useful. But it's created a weird gravitational pull where every roadmap discussion eventually asks "should this have AI in it," even for problems that don't need it.

I went the opposite direction. Over the past year building a 70+ tool image/PDF platform, the actual hard engineering problems weren't "how do we add AI" — they were "how do we remove the server."

The Boring Problem Nobody's Hyping

Most image and PDF tools upload your file to a server, process it there, and send back a result. That's simple, well-understood, and it's also the thing I spent the most engineering effort trying to eliminate — not because servers are bad, but because for a huge category of tools (resize, compress, convert, crop), there's no actual reason a file needs to leave your device at all. Modern browsers can do this work themselves.

No AI model involved. Just Canvas API, a binary search over compression parameters, and a genuinely deterministic result — the same input always produces the same output, which turns out to matter a lot when someone's compressing an ID photo for a government form and needs to trust the tool didn't quietly do something unpredictable to it.

Where I Actually Considered AI, and Didn't Use It

To be fair to the other side of this — I did evaluate AI for a couple of features:

  • Auto-crop/smart framing for passport photos — an AI model could theoretically detect face position and suggest a crop. I shipped a simpler geometric approach instead (detect the largest contiguous skin-tone region, center it) because it's instant, works offline, and — critically — fails predictably. When an AI auto-crop gets it wrong, it's not obvious why. When a rule-based approach gets it wrong, you can usually tell exactly what assumption broke.
  • Smart compression suggestions ("this looks like it could go smaller without visible quality loss") — genuinely tempting to bolt an AI quality-assessment model onto this. Ended up with a much less exciting binary search against a target file size instead, because it's fast enough to run entirely client-side without an API call, and it doesn't need a network connection or ongoing inference cost per use.

Neither decision was "AI bad." Both were "this specific problem doesn't need a probabilistic model when a deterministic one solves it just as well, faster, and for free."

The Uncomfortable Question This Raises

If a meaningful chunk of "let's add AI" decisions in the current wave are driven by genuine capability gaps, that's great — ship it. But I suspect a real chunk of them are driven by something closer to FOMO than by an actual problem AI solves better than existing techniques. Deterministic, boring, well-understood approaches don't get a "Show HN" spike the way "I added AI to my todo app" does, even when the boring approach is objectively the better engineering call for that specific problem.

I don't think this makes AI overrated in general — some categories of problems (genuinely fuzzy classification, natural language understanding, generative tasks) are exactly where it belongs. I think it makes "did I choose AI because it's the right tool, or because it's the interesting one to talk about" a question worth actually asking before shipping, not after.

Where This Landed

The end result is ResizeHub — 70+ tools, no AI anywhere in the pipeline, no server ever touching a file, and it turns out "boring and deterministic" was the harder, more interesting engineering problem the whole time.

Genuinely curious where others have landed on this — have you shipped an AI feature and regretted it, or skipped one and been glad you did? Not looking for an anti-AI pile-on, actually curious about the cases that went either way.
